Every day. Not occasionally, when provoked past endurance. There is nothing in this of a God who loses his temper; it is the steady, daily, moral response of goodness to what evil is doing in his world. Take that away and you have a God who does not care what happens to you.

If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword; he has bent and readied his bow; he has prepared for him his deadly weapons, making his arrows fiery shafts.

The picture is of a warrior arming himself in the open, taking his time, and everything hangs on the first clause: if a man does not repent. The sword is being sharpened where it can be seen, and the door is still open. Judgment in Scripture is always announced before it falls, and always with a way out.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wicked man conceives evil and is pregnant with mischief and gives birth to lies. He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends. I will give to the LORD the thanks due to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the LORD, the Most High.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, the wicked man conceives evil and is pregnant with mischief and gives birth to lies. He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends.

Two pictures, and they are the same point. First, evil gestates: it is conceived, carried, and delivered, which is to say that the lie Cush told had a long private history before anyone heard it. James says it the same way — desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin (Jas 1:15). Nobody wakes up and destroys a reputation before breakfast. It is carried for months.

Second, evil is self-defeating by design. The man digs a pit for someone else and the loose earth gives way under his own feet. Scripture tells this story again and again, most memorably of a gallows built for Mordecai and used for the man who built it. God has built the world so that malice tends to come home, which is not always visible on the day and is one of the reasons the righteous can wait.

Two cautions, because this verse gets misused. It is not a promise that every liar will be publicly exposed in your lifetime; the psalm itself ends with the case still open. And it is not permission to sit and watch for someone's collapse. The man who wrote it had refused twice to dig a pit of his own when Saul was within reach (1 Sam 24:10-11). You cannot pray verse 15 with any honesty while holding a shovel.

I will give to the LORD the thanks due to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the LORD, the Most High.

And the last two words are a title the Psalter has not used before: the LORD, the Most High. Elyon, the one above everything — above Cush, above Saul's court, above the assembly of the peoples the psalm asked God to convene. A man being talked about in a small country names the height of the one he has told about it.

The psalm ends before the verdict does. Nothing has been settled about Cush; the last verse is a man singing anyway, thanking God for being the kind of God who judges rightly. That is what it looks like to leave a case with him: not silence, not brooding, but praise offered before the outcome is known.

8.title: What Is Man?
8.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Gittith. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! You have set your glory above the heavens.2Out of the mouth of babies and infants, you have established strength because of your foes, to still the enemy and the avenger.3When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place,4what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?5Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor.6You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet,7all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field,8the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, whatever passes along the paths of the seas.9O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!
8.overview: A congregation looks up at the night sky. God's name is majestic in all the earth and his glory is set above the heavens; his answer to his enemies is the noise of infants (vv. 1-2). Seeing the moon and stars, the work of God's fingers, the psalmist asks why God would keep frail man in mind and come to see about him (vv. 3-4). The answer is a coronation: man is set a little lower than the heavenly beings, crowned with glory and honour, given dominion over flocks, beasts, birds and fish (vv. 5-8). The psalm closes on the line it opened with (v. 9).
8.theology:
God defeats the strong with the weak, and Jesus uses v. 2 that way in the temple (Matt 21:15-16), where the Greek text's praise stands in for the Hebrew's strength.

What is man? (v. 4) is answered not with "nothing" but with a crown (v. 5) and a dominion that repeats Gen 1:26-28. Man rules the works of God's hands, which he did not make and cannot sustain: dominion, not ownership.

The dominion is plainly not yet visible, and Hebrews says so, then points to Jesus — made lower for a little while, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:8-9; cf. 1 Cor 15:27; Eph 1:22). The psalm's question is answered by the incarnation: man is the creature God became.
8.examples:
The covenant name and the word for master, in one breath.

Children shouting in the temple courts as God's artillery.

Galaxies as fingerwork.

Mindful: to keep someone deliberately in mind.

Job threw the same question back in bitterness (Job 7:17-18).

Dominion over what God made, not what we made.

We do not yet see ... but we see him (Heb 2:8-9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Out of the Mouth of Babies
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! His glory is above the heavens, and out of the mouths of babies and infants he has established strength against his foes (vv. 1-2). Looking at the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, the psalmist asks: what is man that you are mindful of him? (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: God silences his enemies with infants, and the man who looks up at the stars is asked to notice that God looks down.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! You have set your glory above the heavens. Out of the mouth of babies and infants, you have established strength because of your foes, to still the enemy and the avenger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! You have set your glory above the heavens.

Two different words open the psalm. LORD in capitals is the covenant name God gave to Moses; our Lord is the ordinary word for a master. He is the God who has bound himself to a people and the sovereign who owns them, and the psalm is addressed to him in the plural: our. This is a congregation looking up together.

Out of the mouth of babies and infants, you have established strength because of your foes, to still the enemy and the avenger.

God's chosen weapon against his enemies is the noise small children make. It is the strategy of the whole Bible in one line: God defeats what is strong with what is weak. Jesus quoted this verse, in its Greek form, on the day the temple authorities lost their tempers. Children were shouting Hosanna to the Son of David! in the courts, and when the priests demanded that he silence them he said: have you never read, Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise? (Matt 21:15-16). Where the Hebrew says God establishes strength, the Greek says he prepares praise — and Jesus points at the children and lets the verse make his defence. The strength is the praise.

verseByVerse.quote: When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?

He is outside at night, and the sky is doing to him what it does to everyone: making him feel small. The detail that carries the verse is the work of your fingers. Not his arm, not his shoulder — his fingers. Whole galaxies are God's needlework, a thing done delicately and without strain.

Then the question, and it is the honest one: with all that, why would you give a thought to us? The word for man here is the one that stresses frailty — mortal, breakable. Mindful means to keep someone in mind, to remember them deliberately; care for is the word for visiting, coming to see about someone. So: why do you think about us, and why do you come?

Job took these same words and threw them back in bitterness — What is man, that you make so much of him ... visit him every morning? (Job 7:17-18) — meaning, why will you not leave me alone? The identical question can be asked in wonder or in agony, and Scripture prints both. Here it is wonder. A man who feels insignificant under a night sky is not being told he is nothing; he is being asked to notice that the one who made the stars has him personally in mind.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Crowned with Glory and Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor, giving him dominion over sheep and oxen, beasts, birds and fish (vv. 5-8). The psalm closes with the line it opened with: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The crown given to man in Genesis is worn in full by one man, and the New Testament says so (Heb 2:8-9).

verseByVerse.quote: Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor. You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, whatever passes along the paths of the seas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor. You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, whatever passes along the paths of the seas.

The answer to what is man is not "nothing much". It is a coronation. The ESV notes the line can be read "a little lower than God", and that the Greek Old Testament has "than the angels"; either way the point is that the frail creature of verse 4 is placed astonishingly high and crowned. Genesis said the same thing in prose: made in God's image, told to have dominion over the fish and the birds and every living thing (Gen 1:26-28). The psalm even keeps the livestock and the wild animals and the birds and the fish in view.

Notice that the heavens were the work of your fingers and this dominion is over the works of your hands. Man is given charge of things God made, not things man made; a king over a kingdom he did not create and cannot sustain. That is the difference between dominion and ownership, and forgetting it is most of what has gone wrong with the way we handle the world.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!

The psalm ends on the line it started with, which is the right shape: the middle is about us, and both ends are about him. Whatever glory man has is on loan and reflects back.

But a Christian cannot read verses 5-8 without the ache. All things under his feet? Look around. We cannot govern our own appetites, let alone the seas. The writer to the Hebrews quotes this psalm in full, then says exactly that: At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone (Heb 2:8-9).

There is the answer to the psalm's question, and it is better than the question. What is man? Man is the creature God became. The crown Adam threw away is on the head of the Son of Man, and he did not seize it — he came down to where the frail and breakable are, went lower than any of us in death, and was crowned there. Paul takes the same line to its end: God put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church (Eph 1:22). Nothing in the universe is outside that rule, and the head of it loves you. Go outside and look up, and say the first line again.

9.title: A Stronghold for the Oppressed
9.text: To the choirmaster: according to Muth-labben. A Psalm of David. 1I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart; I will recount all of your wonderful deeds.2I will be glad and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High.3When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish before your presence.4For you have maintained my just cause; you have sat on the throne, giving righteous judgment.5You have rebuked the nations; you have made the wicked perish; you have blotted out their name forever and ever.6The enemy came to an end in everlasting ruins; their cities you rooted out; the very memory of them has perished.7But the LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice,8and he judges the world with righteousness; he judges the peoples with uprightness.9The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.10And those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you.11Sing praises to the LORD, who sits enthroned in Zion! Tell among the peoples his deeds!12For he who avenges blood is mindful of them; he does not forget the cry of the afflicted.13Be gracious to me, O LORD! See my affliction from those who hate me, O you who lift me up from the gates of death,14that I may recount all your praises, that in the gates of the daughter of Zion I may rejoice in your salvation.15The nations have sunk in the pit that they made; in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught.16The LORD has made himself known; he has executed judgment; the wicked are snared in the work of their own hands. Higgaion. Selah17The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations that forget God.18For the needy shall not always be forgotten, and the hope of the poor shall not perish forever.19Arise, O LORD! Let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you!20Put them in fear, O LORD! Let the nations know that they are but men! Selah
9.overview: David gives thanks with his whole heart: God has taken the judgment seat, his enemies have stumbled, nations have been rebuked and whole cities rooted out until even their memory is gone (vv. 1-6). But the LORD sits enthroned forever, judging the world in righteousness and standing as a stronghold for the oppressed, remembered by all who know his name (vv. 7-10). He avenges blood and does not forget the cry of the afflicted (vv. 11-12). So the psalmist asks to be lifted from the gates of death to the gates of Zion (vv. 13-14). The nations sink in the pit they dug, the needy will not always be forgotten, and the psalm ends asking that the nations be made to know that they are only men (vv. 15-20).
9.theology:
Psalms 9 and 10 are one acrostic poem in two moods (see the ESV's note): God has judged, and God seems absent. Both belong in the same book and the same believer.

God's throne outlasts every power whose memory has perished (vv. 6-7), and that permanence is what makes him a stronghold for the oppressed (v. 9). Trust follows knowledge of his name (v. 10).

Blood cries out and is heard (v. 12; Gen 4:10; Rev 6:10), and evil is snared in its own work (vv. 15-16). The psalm concedes that the needy are forgotten NOW and denies that they always will be (v. 18) — which is where Psalm 10 begins. The final petition is that the nations learn they are only men (v. 20; cf. Rev 11:15).
9.examples:
Two psalms, one alphabet: the ESV's note on 9 and 10.

Praise as a decision with a list attached.

The empire that wanted to be remembered, forgotten.

A stronghold: a high place, out of reach of the people below.

The gates of death and the gates of Zion, one verse apart.

Not always forgotten — a time limit on injustice.

The prayer that nations learn they are men.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The LORD Sits Enthroned Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart: his enemies have stumbled and perished, the nations are rebuked, whole cities rooted out (vv. 1-6). But the LORD sits enthroned forever, judging the world with righteousness, a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble (vv. 7-10). Sing to him, for he who avenges blood is mindful of them; he does not forget the cry of the afflicted (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The throne that outlasts empires is the refuge of people with no power at all.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart; I will recount all of your wonderful deeds. I will be glad and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High. When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish before your presence. For you have maintained my just cause; you have sat on the throne, giving righteous judgment. You have rebuked the nations; you have made the wicked perish; you have blotted out their name forever and ever. The enemy came to an end in everlasting ruins; their cities you rooted out; the very memory of them has perished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the choirmaster: according to Muth-labben. A Psalm of David.

The ESV's note tells us something that changes how this psalm is read: Psalms 9 and 10 together run through the Hebrew alphabet, stanza by stanza, and in the Greek Old Testament they are a single psalm. So this is half a poem. The half in front of us is full of thanksgiving that God has judged; the half that follows asks why he is standing far off. Anyone who has swung between those two in a single week is holding the right book.

I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart; I will recount all of your wonderful deeds. I will be glad and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High.

Four verbs, all first person and all deliberate: thanks, recount, exult, sing. Praise here is not a mood that arrives; it is a decision, with a memory attached — he is going to recount, to go through the list.

When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish before your presence. For you have maintained my just cause; you have sat on the throne, giving righteous judgment. The Judge of Psalm 7 has taken his seat and ruled. Nations are rebuked, cities rooted out, the very memory of them gone (vv. 5-6). The verse that tells you how thoroughly is the one about memory: the empire that meant to be remembered forever is not remembered at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice, and he judges the world with righteousness; he judges the peoples with uprightness. The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble. And those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you. Sing praises to the LORD, who sits enthroned in Zion! Tell among the peoples his deeds! For he who avenges blood is mindful of them; he does not forget the cry of the afflicted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice, and he judges the world with righteousness; he judges the peoples with uprightness.

But. Cities fall and their memory perishes; God is still seated. The contrast is the argument: everything that looked permanent has gone, and the throne has not moved.

The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble. And those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you.

A stronghold is a high place, out of reach of the people below. That is the word given to the ones with the least power in the psalm — the oppressed, the crushed, the ones who cannot fight back. And notice the order of trust: those who know your name trust you. Trust is not a leap in the dark; it grows out of knowing who God is, which is why learning what he is like is never a luxury.

Sing praises to the LORD, who sits enthroned in Zion! Tell among the peoples his deeds!

Two commands, and the second is the surprising one. The nations have just been rebuked and rooted out (v. 5), and now the psalmist tells his people to go and tell those same nations what God has done. Israel's praise was never meant to stay indoors. God is enthroned in Zion, a particular hill in a particular city, and the news about him is for everyone — which is the line that runs straight to a command given on another hill outside the same city, to make disciples of all nations.

For he who avenges blood is mindful of them; he does not forget the cry of the afflicted.

This goes back to the first murder, when God told Cain, The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground (Gen 4:10). Spilled blood has a voice, and God hears it. It runs forward too, to the martyrs under the altar crying how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (Rev 6:10). Every violence done to the powerless is on a record God keeps and will settle. To the person who has been hurt and never heard an apology: he does not forget the cry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Let the Nations Know That They Are But Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be gracious to me, O LORD! See my affliction — lift me from the gates of death that I may praise you in the gates of Zion (vv. 13-14). The nations have sunk in the pit they made and are snared in the work of their own hands (vv. 15-16). The wicked return to Sheol, but the needy shall not always be forgotten (vv. 17-18). Arise, O LORD! ... Let the nations know that they are but men! (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Two gates, two destinies, and a prayer that the nations would remember what they are.

verseByVerse.quote: Be gracious to me, O LORD! See my affliction from those who hate me, O you who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may recount all your praises, that in the gates of the daughter of Zion I may rejoice in your salvation. The nations have sunk in the pit that they made; in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught. The LORD has made himself known; he has executed judgment; the wicked are snared in the work of their own hands. Higgaion. Selah The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations that forget God. For the needy shall not always be forgotten, and the hope of the poor shall not perish forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be gracious to me, O LORD! See my affliction from those who hate me, O you who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may recount all your praises, that in the gates of the daughter of Zion I may rejoice in your salvation.

Two gates, one verse apart. He has been at the gates of death — the entrance to the grave, near enough to touch the door — and what he asks is to stand instead in the gates of the daughter of Zion, the city gateway where people met, traded, gave evidence and sang. From the doorway of death to the doorway of the city of God. That is the distance salvation covers, and the reason he wants it is to praise where people can hear him.

The nations have sunk in the pit that they made; in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught. The LORD has made himself known; he has executed judgment; the wicked are snared in the work of their own hands.

The pit of Psalm 7 again, dug now by empires rather than by one liar, with the same result. And the comment on it is the important line: the LORD has made himself known. God is revealed by how history ends up, not only by what he says.

The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations that forget God.

Not the nations that fight God: the nations that FORGET him. That is how most people and most cultures leave God, not by argument but by distraction, until he simply does not come up. And return is a terrible word here, because it makes the grave the place they were always heading back to. A life organised without God ends where it started, in the dust, and that is the plain teaching of the verse. It is also exactly what the gospel exists to reverse: Christ went into that place and came out, and took the keys with him.

For the needy shall not always be forgotten, and the hope of the poor shall not perish forever. Hold that word always. It concedes that they are forgotten now. The psalm is not pretending; it is putting a time limit on the injustice. And that concession is exactly where the next psalm begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD! Let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you! Put them in fear, O LORD! Let the nations know that they are but men! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Arise, O LORD! Let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you! Put them in fear, O LORD! Let the nations know that they are but men!

The last prayer is not that the nations be destroyed but that they be told the truth about themselves. All the damage done in this psalm was done by people who had forgotten they were people: mortal, accountable, made. To know you are but men is the beginning of sanity for an individual and for a government.

And one day the announcement will be made publicly: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever (Rev 11:15). Until then the church prays Psalm 9's last line over every power that thinks it is more than dust, and prays it for herself first.

10.title: Why Do You Stand Far Away?
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?<sup>2</sup>In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised.<sup>3</sup>For the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain curses and renounces the LORD.<sup>4</sup>In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, "There is no God."<sup>5</sup>His ways prosper at all times; your judgments are on high, out of his sight; as for all his foes, he puffs at them.<sup>6</sup>He says in his heart, "I shall not be moved; throughout all generations I shall not meet adversity."<sup>7</sup>His mouth is filled with cursing and deceit and oppression; under his tongue are mischief and iniquity.<sup>8</sup>He sits in ambush in the villages; in hiding places he murders the innocent. His eyes stealthily watch for the helpless;<sup>9</sup>he lurks in ambush like a lion in his thicket; he lurks that he may seize the poor; he seizes the poor when he draws him into his net.<sup>10</sup>The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might.<sup>11</sup>He says in his heart, "God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it."<sup>12</sup>Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up your hand; forget not the afflicted.<sup>13</sup>Why does the wicked renounce God and say in his heart, "You will not call to account"?<sup>14</sup>But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless.<sup>15</sup>Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call his wickedness to account till you find none.<sup>16</sup>The LORD is king forever and ever; the nations perish from his land.<sup>17</sup>O LORD, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart; you will incline your ear<sup>18</sup>to do justice to the fatherless and the oppressed, so that man who is of the earth may strike terror no more.
10.overview: The second half of the acrostic begun in Psalm 9 opens with the hardest question: why does God stand far away and hide in times of trouble (v. 1)? A long portrait of the predator follows — arrogant, successful, greedy, sure he will never meet adversity, his mouth full of cursing, lying in ambush like a lion for the poor and the fatherless, and certain in his heart that God has forgotten and will never see (vv. 2-11). The psalmist prays for God to arise (vv. 12-13), then turns on three words: But you do see, and God has always been the helper of the fatherless (v. 14). Break the arm of the wicked (v. 15). The LORD is king forever; he hears, strengthens, and does justice, so that man made of dust will terrify no one any longer (vv. 16-18).
10.theology:
God's apparent absence is put into words rather than denied (v. 1), and the same appearance is read two ways: the believer asks why God hides, the wicked concludes that God has forgotten (v. 11). What a person does with God's silence reveals what he is.

Practical atheism — all his thoughts are, There is no God (v. 4) — is a working assumption rather than an argument, and Paul cites v. 7 as a description of the whole race (Rom 3:14).

The turn is not a change in circumstances but the knowledge that God sees, notes, and takes the case in hand (v. 14). God's first gift to the afflicted is often a strengthened heart (v. 17), and the terrifying man is only dust with a talent for fear (v. 18).
10.examples:
Not absent — standing far away, which is worse.

A creed nobody states: no one is keeping accounts.

Judgments on high, out of his sight: he never looks up.

Patient, professional hunting of people who cannot afford lawyers.

Verse 1 and verse 11: the same silence, two men.

But you do see — a case accepted, not filed.

Man of the earth: soil that learned to frighten people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — He Says in His Heart, God Has Forgotten
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble? (v. 1). The wicked hunts the poor, boasts of his desires, renounces the LORD, and thinks There is no God (vv. 2-4). His ways prosper; he expects never to meet adversity; his mouth is full of cursing (vv. 5-7). He lies in ambush like a lion for the helpless, and says in his heart, God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it (vv. 8-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm lets the predator speak at length, and his creed is not atheism but the assumption that nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble? In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised. For the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain curses and renounces the LORD. In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, "There is no God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?

The previous psalm ended by insisting that the needy will not always be forgotten. This one opens by asking why they are forgotten now. The two are one poem, and this is what the seam between them sounds like: not doubt replacing faith, but faith asking the question out loud.

Note what he does not say. He does not say God is absent; he says God is standing far away, close enough to be seen and not close enough to help, which is somehow harder. If you have prayed that sentence, you are in the Bible.

In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor ... For the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain curses and renounces the LORD. In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, There is no God.

Here is the portrait, and the last line is the key to it. All his thoughts are, There is no God is not a philosophy; it is a working assumption. He has not sat down and disproved anything. He simply runs his life on the basis that no one is keeping accounts, which is a creed held by many people who would tick the box marked believer. The test is not what you would say if asked but what you assume when nobody is looking.

Notice too that the psalm's first petition is tucked inside the description: let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised (v. 2). Before he argues with God about the delay, he has already asked for the one thing he wants, and it is the pit of Psalm 7 again — let the scheme close on the schemer.

verseByVerse.quote: His ways prosper at all times; your judgments are on high, out of his sight; as for all his foes, he puffs at them. He says in his heart, "I shall not be moved; throughout all generations I shall not meet adversity." His mouth is filled with cursing and deceit and oppression; under his tongue are mischief and iniquity. He sits in ambush in the villages; in hiding places he murders the innocent. His eyes stealthily watch for the helpless; he lurks in ambush like a lion in his thicket; he lurks that he may seize the poor; he seizes the poor when he draws him into his net. The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might. He says in his heart, "God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His ways prosper at all times; your judgments are on high, out of his sight; as for all his foes, he puffs at them. He says in his heart, I shall not be moved; throughout all generations I shall not meet adversity.

Two things make him unbearable: he is successful, and he is untroubled. God's judgments are on high, out of his sight — far above his eye level, so he never looks up. And he has convinced himself of permanence. Every generation has men who believe their arrangement will never be disturbed.

And there is a small, ugly detail in the middle: as for all his foes, he puffs at them. He blows at opposition the way you blow dust off a table. Contempt is the tell. A man who is frightened of nobody has usually stopped believing that anyone, including God, can call him in.

His mouth is filled with cursing and deceit and oppression; under his tongue are mischief and iniquity. Paul puts this verse into his catalogue of what human beings are like without God: Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness (Rom 3:14). The psalm's monster is a portrait of the race, in its natural direction.

He sits in ambush in the villages; in hiding places he murders the innocent ... he lurks in ambush like a lion in his thicket ... The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might.

The hunting imagery is patient and professional: sitting, watching, lurking, netting. This is not a man who loses his temper; it is a man who plans. And the victims are always the same sort: the poor, the helpless, the fatherless. Predators pick targets who cannot afford lawyers.

He says in his heart, God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it.

Read that beside verse 1. The psalmist asked, why do you hide yourself? The wicked man declares, he has hidden his face. The same appearance, and two completely different men: one takes it to God as a question, the other takes it as a licence. What you do with God's apparent silence is one of the truest tests of what you are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up your hand; forget not the afflicted (vv. 12-13). But you do see — God notes mischief and takes it in hand, and has been the helper of the fatherless (v. 14). Break the arm of the wicked (v. 15). The LORD is king forever and ever; he hears the desire of the afflicted and does justice, so that man who is of the earth may strike terror no more (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Three words turn the poem: you do see. The God who seemed far away has been holding the fatherless all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up your hand; forget not the afflicted. Why does the wicked renounce God and say in his heart, "You will not call to account"? But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless. Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call his wickedness to account till you find none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up your hand; forget not the afflicted. Why does the wicked renounce God and say in his heart, You will not call to account?

Watch the hands in this psalm. The wicked man's arm crushes the helpless (v. 10) and the psalmist asks God to lift up your hand (v. 12) and later to break that arm (v. 15). It is a plain request for one strength to overpower another, and it is made to God rather than answered in kind.

But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless.

Three words turn the poem. But you do see. Nothing has changed outside; no thunderbolt has fallen. The psalmist simply remembers, against all appearances, that the accounts are being kept. God does not merely notice the mischief — he notes it, takes it into his hands, which is the language of a case being accepted rather than filed.

And then the two clauses that carry the pastoral weight of the psalm: to you the helpless commits himself, and you have been the helper of the fatherless. Present tense and past tense, faith and evidence. The helpless man has nowhere else to hand himself over, and the record shows where the fatherless have always been able to go. Anyone with no advocate has the Judge himself.

Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call his wickedness to account till you find none. The arm is the strength that does the crushing in verse 10. He asks for the power to be broken, not for the man to be tortured, and he asks God to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is king forever and ever; the nations perish from his land. O LORD, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart; you will incline your ear to do justice to the fatherless and the oppressed, so that man who is of the earth may strike terror no more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is king forever and ever; the nations perish from his land. O LORD, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart; you will incline your ear to do justice to the fatherless and the oppressed, so that man who is of the earth may strike terror no more.

The poem that began with a God standing far off ends with a King who is not going anywhere, and with three verbs of nearness: he hears, he strengthens, he inclines his ear. Look hard at that middle one: strengthen their heart is often what God does first, before he changes a single circumstance. Courage given to the afflicted is already an answer, though it is not the whole answer.

The nations perish from his land — and the pronoun matters. Every predator in this psalm has been operating on ground that belongs to someone else. He is a squatter with a weapon, and the owner is coming back.

And the last line puts the terrifying man in his place with a pun that does not survive translation: he is man who is of the earth, adam from the adamah, dust from the dust he will go back to. That is the whole of his power. He is soil that learned to frighten people, and he will stop.

The Christian reads it knowing when: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever (Rev 11:15). Until then, the prayer of the fatherless is the prayer that is always heard first.

11.title: The LORD Is in His Holy Temple
11.text: To the choirmaster. Of David. 1In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee like a bird to your mountain,2for behold, the wicked bend the bow; they have fitted their arrow to the string to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart;3if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?4The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man.5The LORD tests the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence.6Let him rain coals on the wicked; fire and sulfur and a scorching wind shall be the portion of their cup.7For the LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds; the upright shall behold his face.
11.overview: Friends are urging David to run: the bow is bent, the arrow is on the string, the shot will come out of the dark, and the foundations of any decent order are collapsing — what can one righteous man do (vv. 1-3)? He does not argue with their facts. He answers with where God is: The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man, and the testing falls on the righteous too, while God hates the man who loves violence (vv. 4-5). Fire, sulphur and scorching wind are the wicked man's cup; the upright have a different one, and the psalm ends with the sight of God's face (vv. 6-7).
11.theology:
The counsel to flee is sensible and is refused, because fear is choosing the refuge: in the LORD I take refuge was already true (v. 1). When the foundations shake, the answer is not a better hiding place but an occupied throne (v. 4; Hab 2:20).

God inspects closely — his eyelids narrow (v. 4) — and he tests the righteous rather than exempting them (v. 5). What he hates is the love of violence, a settled taste, not a single failure.

Everyone drinks a cup (v. 6; Gen 19:24; Rev 20:10). The upright are promised not safety but sight: the upright shall behold his face (v. 7; Matt 5:8; Rev 22:4).
11.examples:
The voice telling him to run is a friend's, and it is right about the facts.

The arrow fitted, the shot from the dark.

If the foundations are destroyed: the mood of a decent person watching the walls crack.

Eyelids narrowing: God leaning in to look.

The LORD tests the righteous — not a fault in the system.

The portion of the cup: everyone is drinking something.

The last word is a face.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — How Can You Say, Flee Like a Bird?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee like a bird to your mountain (v. 1)? The wicked have bent the bow and fitted the arrow to shoot from the dark at the upright (v. 2), and the counsel ends with the question of a collapsing world: if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do? (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The pressure in this psalm comes from friends giving sensible advice, and the advice is to run.

verseByVerse.quote: In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee like a bird to your mountain, for behold, the wicked bend the bow; they have fitted their arrow to the string to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart; if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee like a bird to your mountain, for behold, the wicked bend the bow; they have fitted their arrow to the string to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart; if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?

Read the psalm carefully and you find that the voice being answered is not an enemy's. It is a friend's. People who care about him are saying: get out, take to the hills like a bird off a branch. And their reasons are good. The bow is already bent; the arrow is on the string; the shot will come from the dark, where you cannot see who fired it. That is an accurate description of how the upright usually get hit.

Their argument ends in the sentence that gives the psalm its edge: if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do? When the structures that hold a society upright go — courts that can be bought, laws that mean whatever power says, a king's court run on flattery — what is the point of one honest man? The ESV notes it can also be read as a statement rather than a question, the foundations WILL be destroyed. Either way it is the mood of a decent person watching the load-bearing walls crack.

Notice that David does not dispute the facts. He disputes the conclusion, and he does it with the first four words of the psalm: In the LORD I take refuge. I already have a refuge; why are you offering me a mountain? There are times to flee, and David fled more than once (he hid in caves from Saul for years). This is not a rule against prudence. It is a refusal to let fear pick the refuge.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man (v. 4). He tests the righteous and hates the violent (v. 5); fire, sulphur and scorching wind are the portion of their cup (v. 6). For the LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds; the upright shall behold his face (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The answer to a shaking world is not a better hiding place but an occupied throne — and a face the upright will see.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man. The LORD tests the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man. The LORD tests the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence.

Here is his whole answer, and it is not advice — it is a location. The foundations may be going, but the throne is not in the building. Habakkuk answered a collapsing nation with the same sentence: the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (Hab 2:20).

Then a wonderfully human picture: his eyes see, his eyelids test. The eyelids narrow. It is the look of someone examining closely, leaning in to be sure of what he is seeing. God is not glancing at the world from a distance; he is inspecting it at close range, and the arrow fired from the dark was fired in full light as far as he is concerned.

And then the line that stops any easy reading: The LORD tests the righteous. Not only the wicked. The testing is not a mistake in the system, and it is not evidence that God has looked away; it is part of what he does with the people he loves. What he hates is not the tested man but the one who loves violence — and that is a love, a taste for it, not a single act.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him rain coals on the wicked; fire and sulfur and a scorching wind shall be the portion of their cup. For the LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds; the upright shall behold his face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let him rain coals on the wicked; fire and sulfur and a scorching wind shall be the portion of their cup. For the LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds; the upright shall behold his face.

The imagery is taken from Sodom, where the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire (Gen 19:24), and the New Testament ends the devil's story in a lake of the same two substances (Rev 20:10). The scorching wind is the desert blast that kills crops in a day. And all of it is called the portion of their cup — the measure poured out for a man to drink, his allotted share. Every person is drinking something. This psalm says the choice is not whether you have a cup but what is in it.

Which makes the last line of the psalm the best thing in it. The upright have a different cup, and here is what is in it: the upright shall behold his face. Not safety, not a restored society, not even vindication against the archers — his face. The psalm that began with people shouting at a man to run for the hills ends with him looking God in the eye.

That is the promise Jesus made to the clean-hearted (Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God, Matt 5:8), and it is how the Bible's last chapter describes God's servants: They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads (Rev 22:4). If the foundations are destroyed, the righteous can do this: stay, look up at an occupied throne, and wait for the face.

12.title: The Words of the LORD Are Pure Words
12.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Sheminith. A Psalm of David. 1Save, O LORD, for the godly one is gone; for the faithful have vanished from among the children of man.2Everyone utters lies to his neighbor; with flattering lips and a double heart they speak.3May the LORD cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that makes great boasts,4those who say, "With our tongue we will prevail, our lips are with us; who is master over us?"5"Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise," says the LORD; "I will place him in the safety for which he longs."6The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times.7You, O LORD, will keep them; you will guard us from this generation forever.8On every side the wicked prowl, as vileness is exalted among the children of man.
12.overview: The godly seem to have run out and truthful speech with them: everyone lies to his neighbour with flattering lips and a double heart (vv. 1-2). The psalmist prays against the boasting tongue of men whose creed is With our tongue we will prevail ... who is master over us? (vv. 3-4). Then God speaks, once: because the poor are plundered and the needy groan, I will now arise (v. 5). Against human words the psalm sets God's: pure, like silver refined seven times (v. 6). He will keep and guard his people, though the psalm ends with the wicked still prowling and vileness honoured (vv. 7-8).
12.theology:
"There is no one faithful left" is a real feeling and a false measurement (v. 1; cf. Mic 7:2; 1 Kgs 19:10, 18). The sin of the age is counterfeit speech — flattery, the double heart, and words used as a claim to ownership (vv. 2-4).

God's single utterance in the psalm is provoked not by argument but by the groan of the plundered (v. 5), and he sets the time himself: I will now arise.

Set against alloyed human speech, the words of the LORD are refined silver, purified seven times (v. 6; Prov 30:5) — the one thing a believer can stand on when nothing else said to him can be trusted. The psalm ends unresolved, with the wicked still prowling (v. 8): the promise is held, not yet seen.
12.examples:
A heart and a heart: one for what he says, one for what he means.

Flattery is not kindness; it is saying what will move you.

Who is master over us? — Psalm 2's question in the mouth of talkers.

God answers the groan, not the boast.

Silver refined seven times, printed next to flattering lips.

No hallelujah at the end: vileness still exalted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Save, O LORD, for the godly one is gone; for the faithful have vanished from among the children of man (v. 1). Everyone lies to his neighbour, with flattering lips and a double heart (v. 2). May God cut off flattering lips and boasting tongues — the tongues of men who say, With our tongue we will prevail, our lips are with us; who is master over us? (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: A world where words have come loose from truth, and where speech itself has become a way of claiming to own the place.

verseByVerse.quote: Save, O LORD, for the godly one is gone; for the faithful have vanished from among the children of man. Everyone utters lies to his neighbor; with flattering lips and a double heart they speak. May the LORD cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that makes great boasts, those who say, "With our tongue we will prevail, our lips are with us; who is master over us?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Save, O LORD, for the godly one is gone; for the faithful have vanished from among the children of man. Everyone utters lies to his neighbor; with flattering lips and a double heart they speak.

The complaint is that good people have run out. Micah said it in the same words — The godly has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among mankind (Mic 7:2) — and Elijah said it under a broom tree, I, even I only, am left (1 Kgs 19:10), and was wrong: God had seven thousand he had never mentioned. It is a feeling to be taken seriously and not believed absolutely. When you cannot see a faithful person anywhere, the shortage may be in your line of sight.

What has gone is truthful speech. A double heart is, in Hebrew, a heart and a heart: a man with two of them, one for what he says and one for what he means. Flattery is the form it takes here, and it should be named precisely: flattery is not kindness. It is saying what will move someone, regardless of whether it is true.

May the LORD cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that makes great boasts, those who say, With our tongue we will prevail, our lips are with us; who is master over us?

And there is the creed of the age, in any age: we will win with words. Our lips are our own — we can say what we like, spin what we like, and nobody is over us. It is the politics of the propaganda office and the private language of every person who has ever talked his way out of something. Who is master over us? is the same question the kings asked in Psalm 2, asked now by people whose only weapon is their mouth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — I Will Now Arise, Says the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise, says the LORD; I will place him in the safety for which he longs (v. 5). The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times (v. 6). God will keep and guard them, though the wicked still prowl and vileness is exalted (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Against a world of counterfeit speech God sets his own word, refined seven times — and he speaks it on behalf of the plundered.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise," says the LORD; "I will place him in the safety for which he longs." The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise, says the LORD; I will place him in the safety for which he longs.

God speaks. It is the only time in the psalm, and everything about it is deliberate. He does not answer the boasters; he answers the groan. He gives his reason first — because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan — and he times it himself: I will NOW arise. All through these psalms people have been begging God to get up (7:6; 9:19; 10:12). Here, without being asked in this psalm at all, he says he is getting up.

Note who moves him. Not the psalmist's eloquence; the inarticulate noise of people who have been robbed. If you can manage nothing but a groan, you are making the sound that gets God on his feet.

The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times.

Put this verse where the psalm puts it: directly after a world full of flattering lips, boasting tongues and double hearts. Human words have been shown to be alloy — mixed, adulterated, useful for whatever the speaker wants. God's words are the same substance all the way through, run through the furnace until nothing else is left. Seven times is the number of completeness; there is no impurity remaining to burn out.

That is why a believer can build on a sentence of God when he cannot build on anything else he is being told. Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him (Prov 30:5). In a season of spin, propaganda and flattery, this verse is where you put your weight.

verseByVerse.quote: You, O LORD, will keep them; you will guard us from this generation forever. On every side the wicked prowl, as vileness is exalted among the children of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You, O LORD, will keep them; you will guard us from this generation forever. On every side the wicked prowl, as vileness is exalted among the children of man.

He takes God's refined words and turns them into a promise for people: you will keep them — the poor and needy of verse 5 — and you will guard us. The ESV notes the first can be read "guard him", the single afflicted man of God's own speech. Either way the movement is the same: the word that cannot be corrupted keeps people who can be.

And then the psalm simply stops, with the wicked still walking round the outside and vileness exalted — what is worthless being honoured in public. There is no closing hallelujah. This is one of the honest ones. The God who said I will now arise has not yet arisen visibly, and the believer is left holding a pure word in a filthy generation. That is most of Christian life, and the psalm refuses to pretend otherwise. It has given us the only two things that are steady: God's promise to the plundered, and God's word about everything.

13.title: How Long, O LORD?
13.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?2How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?3Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death,4lest my enemy say, "I have prevailed over him," lest my foes rejoice because I am shaken.5But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation.6I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me.
13.overview: Four times in two verses David asks how long: will God forget him forever, hide his face, leave him turning the problem over in his soul with sorrow all day, and let his enemy stay on top (vv. 1-2)? Then three requests — consider, answer, light up my eyes — lest he die and his enemy claim a victory (vv. 3-4). The psalm turns on one word: But I have trusted in your steadfast love, and ends singing because God has dealt bountifully with him, in the past tense, before anything has changed (vv. 5-6).
13.theology:
Lament is prayer, not complaint: the psalmist says to God the very things the wicked man of Ps 10:11 said about him. The same darkness makes one man bold and the other prayerful, and the difference is the direction of the speech.

His argument for rescue is God's reputation rather than his own comfort (v. 4).

The turn comes from what he stands on, not from what he sees (v. 5), and the final verb is past tense: God has dealt bountifully before the deliverance arrives (v. 6). The question itself goes unanswered here and is still being asked at the end of Scripture (Rev 6:10).
13.examples:
Four how longs: the sound of waiting too long.

The committee that meets in your soul at three in the morning.

Jonathan's eyes brightening over honey (1 Sam 14:27).

His reason: what my enemy will say about you.

One word, but, and the floor changes.

Past tense praise, written before the rescue.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? — and twice more: how long must he carry counsel in his soul and sorrow in his heart, and how long shall the enemy be exalted (vv. 1-2)? Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes, lest he sleep the sleep of death and his enemy claim the victory (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Four complaints, one prayer, and all of it said to God rather than about him.

verseByVerse.quote: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?

Four times in two verses. Nowhere else does the Psalter pile the question up like this, and the repetition is the point: this is what it sounds like inside a head that has been waiting too long. Psalm 6 asked it once and the sentence broke off; here it is finished, and finished again, and again.

Look at what each one names. Being forgotten. Having God's face turned away. And then the two things that make a long trouble unbearable: counsel in my soul — the endless internal committee meeting, turning the problem over at three in the morning and getting nowhere — and sorrow in the heart all the day, the kind that does not lift when the sun comes up. The fourth is the enemy still on top.

The wicked man of Psalm 10 said in his heart that God had forgotten and hidden his face, and it made him bold. A believer says the same two things and it makes him pray. Same darkness, opposite direction: he takes the accusation and turns it into an address. God is not being described here, he is being spoken to, which is the difference between a lament and a grumble.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death, lest my enemy say, "I have prevailed over him," lest my foes rejoice because I am shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death, lest my enemy say, I have prevailed over him, lest my foes rejoice because I am shaken.

After the questions, three short imperatives: look, answer, light up my eyes. The last is a physical picture. When Jonathan was exhausted from battle and ate a little honey, his eyes became bright (1 Sam 14:27). Dull eyes are what you see in a face that has run out; a light in the eye is life coming back. He is asking to be revived before he goes out entirely, and he is honest that he is close.

Then his argument, and it is not about himself. His reason is God's reputation: if I go under, my enemy will say he beat me. Grief makes us small and self-enclosed; faith keeps a wider view even in the dark, and the sufferer here is still thinking about what people will conclude about his God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm turns in one word, and the last verb is past tense: he has already dealt bountifully, before anything visibly changes.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me.

One word turns the psalm: but. Nothing in the circumstances has moved. The enemy is still exalted, the face is still hidden, the sorrow was there all day. What changes is where he plants his feet — your steadfast love, the covenant loyalty of God, which does not rise and fall with his eyesight.

And notice the tenses, because they are the whole lesson. I have trusted: already done. My heart shall rejoice: a promise about the future. He has dealt bountifully with me: past tense, written before any rescue shows up. He is not pretending the trouble has ended. He is reaching back to what God has already done and standing on that until the answer comes.

That is the shape of most Christian perseverance, and the order matters: not feeling, then trust; but trust, then singing, and the feeling catching up somewhere along the way. The question how long does not get answered in this psalm, and it does not get answered in a lot of lives either. It is still being asked at the end of the Bible by the martyrs under the altar (Rev 6:10), and the answer there is the same as the answer here: not yet, and I have not forgotten you, and my steadfast love is what you are standing on.

14.title: There Is None Who Does Good
14.text: To the choirmaster. Of David. 1The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, they do abominable deeds; there is none who does good.2The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God.3They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.4Have they no knowledge, all the evildoers who eat up my people as they eat bread and do not call upon the LORD?5There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous.6You would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge.7Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When the LORD restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.
14.overview: The fool says in his heart that there is no God, and lives accordingly (v. 1). God leans over heaven and searches the whole human race for anyone who understands and seeks him, and the finding is: They have all turned aside ... there is none who does good, not even one (vv. 2-3). The evildoers eat up God's people as casually as bread and never pray (v. 4); then terror takes them, because God is with the generation of the righteous, and the poor man's refuge is the LORD (vv. 5-6). The psalm ends in longing: Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! (v. 7).
14.theology:
The fool is a moral category, not an intellectual one (v. 1; cf. 1 Sam 25:25), and his creed is held in the heart and proved by a way of life.

God conducts the search himself and finds no one (vv. 2-3); Paul quotes the verdict to open his case that the whole world is accountable (Rom 3:10-12). The psalm exempts nobody, the religious reader included.

God stands with the righteous by choice, not because verse 3 has exceptions (v. 5), and the poor man's mocked plans rest on him (v. 6).

Because no one does good, the only hope is rescue from outside: salvation ... out of Zion (v. 7) — which is what came (Rom 3:21-22). Psalm 53 is this psalm again with the divine name changed; the exposition stands here.
14.examples:
Nabal: as his name is, so is he.

A creed held in the heart and proved by the hands.

God leaning over the edge of heaven to look for one seeker.

Eating people the way you eat lunch.

Prayerlessness and using people: one disease, two depths.

The plans of the poor, and who their refuge is.

A groan shaped like a wish — answered out of Zion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Looks Down from Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fool says in his heart, There is no God; they are corrupt and do abominable deeds (v. 1). The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God (v. 2). The verdict: They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: God conducts the search himself, and Paul quotes the result as the Bible's verdict on the whole race (Rom 3:10-12).

verseByVerse.quote: The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, they do abominable deeds; there is none who does good. The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God. They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fool says in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they do abominable deeds; there is none who does good.

The heading is bare — To the choirmaster. Of David — and notice what it means: this flat verdict on the human race was handed to the music director to be sung by the congregation it describes.

The word for fool is not about intelligence. It is a moral word: the man who is closed at the top, who has no room in his scheme for God and behaves accordingly. There is a character in Samuel actually called Nabal, and his wife says of him, as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him (1 Sam 25:25): a rich, drunk, cruel man who cannot see past his own shearing festival.

And the creed is said in his heart, exactly where the predator of Psalm 10 said God had forgotten. This is not a lecture-hall atheism. It is the practical conclusion of a life that has arranged itself as though no one is above it. The proof offered is not an argument but a way of living: corrupt, abominable deeds, nothing good.

The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God.

Now God himself does the surveying. He leans over the edge of heaven and searches the whole human population for one person who is genuinely seeking him — and the language is the language of the search that went on over Sodom, where ten righteous men could not be found. The ESV notes that understand can be read act wisely: this is not clever people versus stupid ones, but people who have their bearings versus people who have lost them.

They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.

That is the finding, and Paul makes it the foundation of the gospel. When he opens his case that the whole world is accountable to God, he quotes these verses almost word for word: None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one (Rom 3:10-12). Read it slowly enough to feel it land on yourself, because the psalm gives no one an exemption. The comfortable religious reader and the fool in verse 1 are in the same survey.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — God Is with the Generation of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The evildoers eat up my people as they eat bread and never call on the LORD (v. 4). There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous (v. 5); they would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge (v. 6). Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm ends not with a solution but with a longing — and the longing is for someone to come out of Zion.

verseByVerse.quote: Have they no knowledge, all the evildoers who eat up my people as they eat bread and do not call upon the LORD? There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous. You would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have they no knowledge, all the evildoers who eat up my people as they eat bread and do not call upon the LORD?

The image is deliberately casual. They consume people the way a man eats his lunch: without cruelty in the moment, without thinking about it at all. Most of the damage done to the poor in any society is done exactly like that, by people who are not plotting anything, just eating. And the tell is in the last clause: they do not call upon the LORD. Prayerlessness and using people are the same disease at two depths.

There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous. You would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge.

There — at some particular point, without warning. The men who had settled it that nobody was watching are suddenly in a terror they cannot account for, because the thing they had ruled out is present: God is with the generation of the righteous. He is not with them because they are impressive; verse 3 has just said nobody is. He is with them because he has chosen to stand there.

And the poor man in verse 6 has plans — small ones, the plans of someone with no leverage — which the powerful would happily laugh at. The psalm says the LORD is his refuge. That is the whole of his security and it is enough, and it is the sentence to give anyone whose plans have been mocked by people with more power than they have.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When the LORD restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When the LORD restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.

The psalm does not end with a fix. It ends with a groan shaped like a wish. If there is none who does good, then no reform will work, no better generation is coming, and the only hope is that salvation arrives from outside — out of Zion, out of the place where God had put his name.

That is precisely what happened. Salvation came out of Zion: a man from Jerusalem's own hill country, crucified outside its wall, who is the one exception to verse 3 and the reason anyone else gets out from under it. Paul quotes this psalm to prove that no one is righteous, and then says, But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law ... through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe (Rom 3:21-22). The psalm asks for it; the gospel reports it.

Say the last line the way it is written, as a prayer that is still partly unanswered — for a restoration not yet complete, in a world still full of verse 4. Jacob will rejoice. It is not yet, and it is certain.

15.title: Who Shall Dwell on Your Holy Hill?
15.text: A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill?2He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart;3who does not slander with his tongue and does no evil to his neighbor, nor takes up a reproach against his friend;4in whose eyes a vile person is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; who swears to his own hurt and does not change;5who does not put out his money at interest and does not take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be moved.
15.overview: Someone at the sanctuary gate asks who may be God's guest and who may live on his hill (v. 1). The answer is a list of eleven marks, almost all of them about how a man treats people: he walks blamelessly, does right, and speaks truth in his heart; he does not slander, harm a neighbour, or carry a reproach about a friend (vv. 2-3); he despises what is vile and honours those who fear the LORD; he keeps a promise that has turned costly; he does not lend at interest or take a bribe against the innocent (vv. 4-5). He who does these things shall never be moved.
15.theology:
The psalm is an entrance liturgy (cf. 24:3-4; Isa 33:14-16), asking both to be a guest in God's tent and to live on his hill (v. 1).

The requirements are moral, not ritual: truth spoken inwardly (v. 2), a tongue that will not carry gossip (v. 3), company chosen by the fear of God rather than by success (v. 4), a promise kept after it proves expensive (v. 4), and money that does not profit from a neighbour's disaster (v. 5; Exod 22:25; Lev 25:36-37; Deut 23:19-20).

Read honestly, the list bars everyone; one man keeps it whole, and believers come to the hill in him (Heb 12:22-24), after which the list describes the life rather than guarding the door.
15.examples:
A question asked at a gate, answered by a priest.

Guest for a night and resident for life, asked at once.

Truth spoken in his heart, where no one can check.

Refusing delivery of a piece of gossip.

The promise that turned expensive and was kept anyway.

No ritual items on the list: the gate is guarded by the neighbours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Question at the Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill? (v. 1). The answer begins: He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart, who does not slander, does no evil to a neighbour, and takes up no reproach against his friend (vv. 2-3).
verseByVerse.theology: The question is about access to God, and the first answers are all about the tongue.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill? He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart; who does not slander with his tongue and does no evil to his neighbor, nor takes up a reproach against his friend;
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill?

This is a question asked at a gate. Worshippers arriving at the sanctuary would ask who may come in, and a priest would answer; Psalm 24 does the same thing at the temple doors, and Isaiah asks it of a fire nobody can live beside (Isa 33:14-16). Two verbs are used, and they ask for different things. To sojourn is to be a guest, to stay in someone's tent for a night under his protection. To dwell is to live there. The psalm wants both: welcome now, and a permanent address.

He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart.

Three summary marks — his walk, his actions, his speech — and the third one goes furthest in. Not speaks truth with his mouth: in his heart. The man is honest at the place where nobody can check, which means he is not lying to himself either. That is rarer than public honesty and it is where public honesty comes from.

Who does not slander with his tongue and does no evil to his neighbor, nor takes up a reproach against his friend.

Notice how much of the entrance requirement is about talk. Takes up a reproach is the picture of picking something up and carrying it — somebody hands you a piece of damaging gossip about a friend and you accept delivery and pass it on. The psalm says: the man who may live with God is the man who refuses the parcel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — He Who Swears to His Own Hurt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He despises what is vile and honours those who fear the LORD; who swears to his own hurt and does not change (v. 4); who lends without interest and takes no bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be moved (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Keeping a costly promise and refusing easy money are the tests, and the man who passes them is immovable.

verseByVerse.quote: in whose eyes a vile person is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; who swears to his own hurt and does not change; who does not put out his money at interest and does not take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In whose eyes a vile person is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; who swears to his own hurt and does not change.

His judgments run the opposite way to the world's. He is not impressed by a successful scoundrel and he does honour ordinary people who fear God, which is precisely the reverse of how most rooms work. Whose company do you actually want? That is a value judgment, and this psalm treats it as a test of fitness for God's presence.

Then the hardest line in the psalm: who swears to his own hurt and does not change. He promised something, it turned out to cost far more than he thought, and he did it anyway. Not renegotiated, not quietly let go, not explained away in the light of new information. Most of us have a clause in our heads that opens when keeping our word gets expensive. The man who lives with God does not.

Who does not put out his money at interest and does not take a bribe against the innocent.

The law forbade lending at interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exod 22:25; Lev 25:36-37; Deut 23:19-20).
